title: Shipping Safely: Accessibility, Web Vitals, Security

scenes.say: Put your mouse in a drawer. Can you still sign up? A clickable div says no. By the end you'll fix it, and dodge the three mistakes interviewers always ask about.

lines.text: No mouse. Can you sign up?

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Make a form work without a mouse. Cut a page load from four seconds to two. And stop X S S, C S R F, cross origin resource sharing, C O R S, mistakes.
lines: Make a form usable without a mouse
Speed up the hero image: LCP 4.1 s to 2.3 s
Stop XSS, CSRF and CORS mistakes

scenes.title: A signup form that fails users
scenes.statement: The signup form is a clickable div with a placeholder-only input. Keyboard and screen reader users cannot use it.
scenes.say: Try our signup form with only a keyboard. Tab to Sign up, press enter, and nothing happens. The goal: the button reached, the field named, every error announced.

scenes.head: What a screen reader hears
scenes.say: Think of an audio guide reading your page aloud. That is a screen reader. For a div with a click handler, it often says group, with no name. No role, and the keyboard cannot reach it. Use a real button, and it says: Sign up, button. Enter and space work for free.

scenes.head: Bug and fix: native elements
scenes.say: On the left, the bug. A div takes no focus and has no role. A placeholder vanishes as you type. It is not a label. Right side, the fix. A label, connected by html for and id, names the field. A real button gives focus, a role, and keyboard activation.

panels.label: fix
panels.code:
<label htmlFor="email">
  Email
</label>
<input id="email" />
<button onClick={go}>
  Sign up
</button>

scenes.head: Focus order and live errors
scenes.say: Now press Tab. Focus should move email, then password, then Sign up, in reading order, with a visible outline. Never remove it. When validation fails, write the message into an A R I A live region, a box screen readers watch. It must already be there. Screen readers read it aloud when it changes. The screen reader announces it, and focus stays put.
Your turn. A div with a click handler sits next to a real button. You press Tab, then Enter. What works? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: A `<div onClick>` and a `<button>`. You press Tab, then Enter.

scenes.head: Only the button takes focus
scenes.say: Only the button. Tab skips the div, because a div cannot take focus. The button gets focus, and Enter clicks it. You can patch a div with tab index, a role, and key handlers. Or write button, and get all of it for free.

scenes.head: The rest of the checklist
scenes.say: Four more details. Never write outline none without a replacement, or keyboard users lose their place. Text contrast: W C A G double A wants four point five to one. Alt text describes purpose, and stays empty if decorative. ARIA only fills gaps. That fixes the form: button reached, field named, errors announced. Test with the keyboard, a screen reader, and axe, an automatic checker.
rows: WCAG AA: 4.5 to 1, large text 3 to 1
ARIA: extra labels for screen readers
native element first; ARIA fills gaps

scenes.title: A hero image that shows late
scenes.statement: On a phone, the big hero image appears after 4.1 seconds. Google wants Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 seconds.
scenes.say: Your laptop says instant. A phone says the hero image is late: Largest Contentful Paint of four point one seconds. Google wants it under two point five.

scenes.head: Core Web Vitals: a restaurant
scenes.say: Core Web Vitals are three numbers. Think restaurant. L C P: the main dish arrives, under two and a half seconds. I N P: the waiter answers your wave, under two hundred milliseconds. C L S: the table jumping while you eat, under zero point one.

scenes.head: LCP, hero image (illustrative)
scenes.say: Illustrative numbers. Before: four point one seconds. The limit: two point five. After a preload: two point three.

scenes.head: When does the browser see the hero?
scenes.say: Why so slow? A script set the hero image. The browser had to download the page, then the script, run it, and only then ask for the image. With a preload, it asks right after the page arrives. The image starts about one point eight seconds earlier.

scenes.head: The fix: preload and size the image
scenes.say: The fix is in the head. Preload says: fetch this image now, at high priority. Give the image tag a width and a height, so the browser reserves its box early. And write alt text.
Predict it. Take away the width and height. The browser has no idea how tall the image is. When it finally loads, what happens to the text below? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `` has no width or height. Text below, after it loads?
scenes.optCue: what happens to the text below

scenes.head: Late content pushes your text
scenes.say: It jumps down. Same story with an ad. You are reading a paragraph. The ad slot above is empty, so it takes no room. Then the ad loads, two hundred fifty pixels tall, and shoves your text down. That is layout shift. The fix: reserve the space up front.

scenes.head: Slow vital, likely cause
scenes.say: Which vital is bad tells you where to look. Slow L C P? Preload the hero and compress images. Slow I N P? Break long scripts into small tasks. High C L S? Reserve space for images and ads. Never lazy load the hero. So it lands near two point three seconds.
rows: split long scripts into small tasks
set image sizes; reserve ad space
delays LCP: lazy only below the fold

scenes.title: A comment that runs code
scenes.statement: Users post comments and you render them. One comment is an image tag with a script on its error handler.
scenes.say: Imagine a comment box. A user posts an image tag with a script on its error handler. The goal: plain text, never run.

scenes.head: Cross-site scripting in four steps
scenes.say: Cross site scripting, X S S, in four steps. An attacker posts the comment. Your server saves it as is. A victim opens the page. The browser reads the comment as H T M L. The script runs, as the victim, on your site.

scenes.head: Text, not HTML
scenes.say: Inner H T M L parses the string, so the script runs. Text content treats it as plain text. Or escape the angle brackets yourself, and it prints harmless text. React escapes for you, unless you reach for dangerously set inner H T M L. As a second layer, add a Content Security Policy: a server header that says which scripts may run.
Your turn. A comment contains bold tags around the word hi. We set text content to it. What does the user see? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: innerHTML vs textContent
scenes.say: The tags, as text. Text content never parses. Inner H T M L would show hi in bold, and with an onerror attribute, it would run code. Same string, two very different pages.

items.label: innerHTML parses it
items.cue: Inner H T M L would

arrows.cue: Inner H T M L would

scenes.head: CSRF: a forged transfer
scenes.say: Cross site request forgery, C S R F. You log in to your bank, which sets a cookie. Later you open evil dot com, which quietly submits a form to the bank. The browser attaches your cookie, so the bank sees you. Money moves.

scenes.head: The attack, and the cookie defense
scenes.say: Here is the attack. A form on evil dot com posts to the bank. The browser adds your cookie. The defense sits on the bank's side. HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts. SameSite Lax makes the browser skip it on a cross site post. Add a C S R F token too, a secret the attacker cannot read.

panels.label: defense
panels.code:
Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly;
            SameSite=Lax

<input type="hidden"
  name="csrf" value="x7Qp">

steps.cue: Add a C S R F token

scenes.head: XSS vs CSRF, and the classic mistakes
scenes.say: X S S runs script on your site: escape output and add a policy. C S R F forges requests: same site cookies and tokens. A token in local storage? Any X S S can read it, so use an HttpOnly cookie. And never change data on a GET. So for X S S: plain text, never run.
rows: XSS: script runs on your site
any XSS reads it: HttpOnly cookie
Lax still sends GET: use POST

scenes.title: The browser blocks my API call
scenes.statement: Your page on app.com calls api.com. The console says the request was blocked by CORS.
scenes.say: Ever seen blocked by C O R S in your console? Your page on app dot com calls api dot com. We want the script to read the response.

scenes.head: Same-origin policy and the opt-in
scenes.say: An origin is scheme, host, and port. By default, a page on app dot com cannot read responses from api dot com. The server opts in with a header, Access Control Allow Origin. If it names the page, the browser lets the script read the response. If not, the browser blocks it. That protects you: sites cannot read each other's data.

scenes.head: The preflight question
scenes.say: Some requests get a question first. A put, or a custom header, is not simple. So the browser sends an options request, the preflight. It asks: may app dot com use put? The server answers with allow headers. Only then does the real request go.

panels.code:
OPTIONS /orders HTTP/1.1
Origin: https://app.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: content-type

scenes.say: Predict it. The server sends no CORS headers at all. A simple GET from app dot com goes out. What does your script see? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: api.com sends no CORS headers. A GET from app.com goes out. Script sees?

scenes.head: Sent, answered, then withheld
scenes.say: A CORS error and no body. The request did reach the server, and the server answered. The browser withheld the answer, because the header is missing. That is why curl works while the browser fails. And the fix lives on the server.

scenes.head: CORS mistakes
scenes.say: Three mistakes. Fixing C O R S in React? Not a frontend fix. The server sends headers. Star origin with cookies? Rejected, so name the origin. And C O R S as security? It protects browsers only. A dev proxy hides the error locally.
rows: not a frontend fix: the server sends the header

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Accessibility basics? Semantic H T M L first: real buttons, labels, alt text. Everything works by keyboard, with visible focus. ARIA only fills gaps. How do you test? Keyboard only, a screen reader, and axe or Lighthouse.
rows: all by keyboard, visible focus; ARIA fills gaps
keyboard, screen reader, axe or Lighthouse

scenes.say: Self-test. Normal body text, W C A G double A. What contrast ratio do you need? Pause and answer.
scenes.q: WCAG AA contrast for normal text?

scenes.say: Four point five to one, for normal text. Low-vision readers need that extra contrast. Alt text? Purpose, empty if decorative. Common mistake? Clickable divs, and outline none.
lines: Alt text? Purpose; empty if decorative
Common mistake? Clickable divs, outline none

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What are Core Web Vitals? Three numbers: load, response, stability. L C P? Under two and a half seconds: preload the hero. I N P? Click to next paint, under two hundred milliseconds: split big scripts. C L S? Under zero point one: set sizes, reserve space.
rows: LCP, INP, CLS: load, response, stability
click to next paint; < 200 ms: split big scripts

scenes.say: Self-test. Before the real request, the browser sends a preflight. Which HTTP method does it use? Pause and answer.
scenes.q: Which HTTP method is the CORS preflight?

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: The answer is OPTIONS, the preflight method. X S S versus C S R F? X S S runs script. Escape output, add a policy. C S R F forges requests: same site cookies and tokens.
rows: script on your site vs forged request

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is C O R S? Browsers block cross origin reads unless opted in. Why a preflight? The browser asks first with options, for non simple requests. Fix a C O R S error? The server sends the right headers.
rows: browser blocks cross-origin reads unless opted in
cues: What is C O R S
Fix a C O R S

scenes.head: Try these
scenes.say: Three exercises. Unplug your mouse, and sign up on your form. Run Lighthouse, and preload the hero. Then try posting an image tag with onerror in a comment box.
rows: Sign up on your own form with Tab only
Run Lighthouse; preload the hero image
Post `` in your comment box

scenes.say: So say this. Native elements first, keyboard everywhere, test with a screen reader. Vitals: L C P, I N P, C L S, each with one fix. Escape output. Same site cookies. Let the server set C O R S.
lines: Native HTML first. Keyboard works everywhere.
LCP, INP, CLS: preload, split, reserve space.
Escape output. SameSite cookies. Server sets CORS.
